title: Technical QA playbook: inference risks and attack scenarios
content:
Purpose:
This note is a field-facing technical QA playbook for Solutions Engineers and Technical Sellers. It focuses on common claims made by prospects or self-hosted vendors (vLLM, Text Generation Inference, TensorRT-LLM stacks) and provides crisp, repeatable rebuttals, diagnostics, and migration prompts. Use as a script during discovery and to prepare tailored demos or proof-of-concepts.

Elevator framing (30s):
- What they say: "We can run models in-house with open frameworks and save money."
- What to answer: "Open stacks can be economical, but they shift complexity to ops and dev teams — patching, kernel tuning, KV caching, model variance management, and SLOs. Redwood's value is predictable unit economics, operational controls (canary rollouts, automatic fallback), and a performance-optimized runtime that reduces engineering toil and outage risk."

Discovery checklist (questions to surface risk/cost):
- Traffic shape: steady vs spiky? peak QPS and average QPS?
- Typical sequence length distribution (median, 95th, worst-case).
- P95 latency SLO targets (50ms/100ms/500ms?).
- Concurrency (number of parallel requests with KV cache warm).
- Do you require streaming responses, function/tool calling, or structured outputs?
- Data residency and compliance constraints (VPC, on-prem, HSM/KMS?).
- Internal team: SRE headcount for model infra, expected on-call rotations, SLA tolerance.

Common competitor claims and counters:
1) Claim: "We run vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM and achieve similar latency at lower cost."
   Rebuttal:
   - Check workload parity: many open-stack numbers are for idealized payloads (short sequences, single model, warm cache). Real apps have variable seq lengths and multiple models; kernel selection and memory fragmentation materially impact throughput.
   - Hidden costs: engineering hours for kernel integration (TRT/PTX), maintaining Triton or custom schedulers, security patches, and alerts/action runbooks. Translate into FTE-months and show cost vs Redwood's appliance.
   - Feature gaps: rollout controls (canaries/A-B), safe fallback when models OOM, multi-tenant routing policies — typically missing or custom-built.

2) Claim: "Open is more flexible — no vendor lock-in."
   Rebuttal:
   - Flexibility is real, but operational burden is non-trivial. Ask: who will own model upgrades, quantization regressions, and drift detection? If they expect platform teams to handle it, quantify the team commitment.
   - Show Redwood's migration hooks: container images for Private, model export/import compatibility, and well-documented rollback semantics to reduce perceived lock-in.

3) Claim: "We can match token costs with FP16/INT8 quantization and Triton optimizations."
   Rebuttal:
   - Quantization tradeoffs: regressions in quality for some model families; need per-prompt evals. Redwood Optimize gives quantization recommendations per workload plus eval monitoring.
   - Kernel maturity: TensorRT INT8 kernels for some ops are fast, but operator coverage and memory planning for KV cache are often partial. This causes OOMs or forced batching strategies that increase p95 latency.

Technical diagnostics to run in a discovery POC:
- Baseline measurement script: 95th percentile latency per token for sequence lengths {32,128,512}. Report GPU UTIL, GPU MEM, host CPU, and batching latency.
- Cold vs warm cache runs: measure penalty when KV cache cold and on first token.
- Multi-model churn test: simulate N different model IDs requested uniformly to show throughput degradation.
- Failure mode tests: run intentionally large context to provoke OOM and observe fallbacks.
- Network and ingress shaping: measure p95 under tail-latency noise from noisy neighbors.

Quantitative callouts to use (examples you can quote when backed by bench):
- Typical managed-to-selfhosted delta: 20–40% higher total cost when accounting for ops and SRE for production-grade deployments at non-trivial scale. (Frame as "depends on traffic shape; we can run estimator during the POC").
- Latency reality: Self-hosted stacks often report median throughput numbers; the p95 (user-visible) can be 2–4x worse depending on batching strategy and cache hit-rate.

Risk catalog and mitigation scripts (how to respond):
- Risk: Operator fatigue from chasing kernel regressions.
  Mitigation: Outline a maintenance cadence and propose Redwood Dedicated or Private with managed kernel patches and release notes. Offer a 90-day migration pilot.
- Risk: Security/compliance pushback on outbound API.
  Mitigation: Walk through Redwood Private options (VPC, on-prem), KMS integration, and audit log examples. Offer architecture diagram for PRD.
- Risk: Performance regressions after model upgrades.
  Mitigation: Propose Redwood's canary rollout + eval gating; show example alert that triggers automatic rollback on quality drift.

Migration playbook (high-level, to share with engineering buyer):
1) Baseline: run the diagnostic scripts above for 2 models and 2 sequence buckets.
2) Cost parity run: run cost-estimator with ops overhead assumptions (FTE, monitoring, storage, backup).
3) Pilot: deploy a subset of traffic to Redwood (10–20%) or Redwood Private in their VPC for 4 weeks.
4) Verify: SLOs, cost, and regression alarms.
5) Rollout: gradual increase with canary windows, automated fallback policy.

Demo/POC checklist for SEs:
- Pre-POC: collect real prompt traces (anonymized) and token distributions.
- POC infra: define traffic shape (QPS, concurrency, sequence len mix).
- Success criteria: p95 latency target, cost per 1M tokens including ops estimate, and no functional regressions (semantic checks on prompts).
- Data handling confirmation: where logs live, retention, PIIs redaction.

Objection handling scripts (short):
- "We don't want managed lock-in." -> "Redwood supports standard model formats, exports, and private deployments. Our win is operational burden reduction; you keep choice over models and can export the artifacts."
- "We already have devs for infra." -> "Great—let's quantify their capacity. Many teams underestimate the oncall and kernel maintenance time; if you'd like, we can model the headcount impact for your team in a 12-month TCO."

Attack scenarios (scripts to call out to customer if vendor X claims):
- Scenario A: Vendor claims "no vendor libs, pure open-source". Ask for timelines on kernel updates, who will own security patches, and evidence of multi-model production deployments at scale. Request the last 3 production incidents and the RCA.
- Scenario B: Vendor provides dazzling microbenchmarks. Ask for the exact request shape and whether experiments include multi-tenant and cold-warm transitions. Also request real p95 numbers from a comparable customer.

Field collateral to attach in the follow-up email:
- Lightweight benchmark deck (3 slides) with p50/p95 examples for short/medium/long sequences.
- Cost estimator spreadsheet pre-populated with FTE multipliers and hardware refresh schedule.
- Migration checklist and runbook template for on-prem/private pilots.

Appendix: quick technical talking points
- Batching vs latency: larger batch sizes improves throughput but increases p95 latency; continuous batching can help but requires careful SLO tuning.
- KV cache: In-generation KV caching reduces token compute significantly for multi-turn chat — but requires runtime support to manage memory on GPU. Self-hosted stacks often lack a battle-tested cache eviction strategy.
- Quantization caveat: INT8 helps TCO but needs per-model evals and custom calibrations; not drop-in for all models.
- Kernel/driver fragility: New CUDA/TensorRT versions can regress perf; managed vendors validate across a matrix and provide fallbacks.

Next steps (SE playbook):
1) Run the discovery checklist in first 15 minutes of call.
2) If prospect has >100 QPS peak or p95 <200ms target, recommend a benchmark pilot.
3) Send follow-up with benchmark deck, cost estimator, and a proposed 4-week pilot plan.

Notes/ownership:
- Owner: Priya Kapoor (GTN SE materials).
- Suggested review: Solutions Engineering, Product (Hosted API + Private), Applied ML infra.
- Status: draft — please add region-specific regulatory callouts and any customer anonymized case studies for the benchmark deck.
